summary:
Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies. Schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. That release initiated the court challenge.

The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 was passed with the province invoking the notwithstanding clause, a five-year override of the Charter. It requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the invocation of the clause may prevent legal action from succeeding on Charter grounds.

On 11 August 2025 the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan (2025 SKCA 74) set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. The appeal court held that Charter breaches under sections 1 and 15 cannot be tested where section 33 has been invoked. Reporting on the same judgment states that the appeal was granted in part, that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench.

Amnesty International Canada participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada. Amnesty argued that courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down, and that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both the province and UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.
tangentialFactors:
The provincial government argued that its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. The Court of Appeal granted that appeal in part on 11 August 2025 while allowing litigation to continue, and both sides then appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, so the dispute is unresolved at the date of the latest source, 6 November 2025.

The request to expedite Saskatchewan's case was made together with the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21, placing the province's pronoun-notice measure among the constitutional matters the highest court was asked to take up on an accelerated schedule.

The pronoun-notice policy has been in force since 2023 while the litigation runs; counsel for the respondents stated in August 2025 that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the provincial human rights complaints route for discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, and legal gender change is handled under Saskatchewan's own provincial rules.

For residents with school-age children, the parental inclusion and consent policies and the Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 require parental consent before a student under 16 uses a gender-related preferred name or gender identity at school, and require parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum.

Saskatchewan is one of three provinces, with British Columbia and Ontario, that will grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing a wider range of queer and trans families.

Human rights groups have called for repeal of the 2023 measure, and the legal action they supported continues in the Court of King's Bench pending the Supreme Court of Canada hearing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources describing the 11 August 2025 judgment differ in emphasis and are not fully reconcilable from the inventory: one reports that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches where section 33 was invoked and that the policy stands, the other reports the appeal granted in part with a judge retaining jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights. This is unresolved.

No Saskatchewan-specific correctional placement rule or case is documented in the inventory; provincial correctional policies are described only as varying. The placement policy and custody statistics available are national in scope and are not carried here.

No trans-specific violence, homicide or assault figure for Saskatchewan is sourced, and no dated incident of violence against a trans person in the province appears in the inventory. Nothing about present violence levels can be stated either way.

The procedural detail of legal gender change in Saskatchewan, including evidence requirements, waiting periods and processing times, is not sourced. Entry, visa, identity-document marker and airport-screening rules are national matters and are not documented for this province.

Beyond the 6 November 2025 announcement that the Supreme Court of Canada will hear the appeals, no hearing date, no merits ruling and no outcome is documented; the policy's constitutionality was undecided at that date.

The available public-opinion figures on transgender tolerance are national, were collected in 2020, and are not Saskatchewan-specific, so they are not carried in this record.
